claim: Down syndrome (DS) is characterized by skeletal and brain structural malformations, cognitive impairment, altered hippocampal metabolite concentration and gene expression imbalance.
source: Down syndrome (DS) is characterized by skeletal and brain structural malformations, cognitive impairment, altered hippocampal metabolite concentration and gene expression imbalance.
evidence: This is a general statement about DS characteristics that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Ts65Dn mouse model reflected the pleiotropic nature of DS, exhibiting brachycephalic skull, ventriculomegaly, neurodevelopmental delay, hyperactivity, and impaired memory robustness with altered hippocampal metabolite concentration and gene expression.
source: Our findings revealed that the Ts65Dn mouse model reflected the pleiotropic nature of DS, exhibiting brachycephalic skull, ventriculomegaly, neurodevelopmental delay, hyperactivity, and impaired memory robustness with altered hippocampal metabolite concentration and gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including imaging, behavioral tests, MRS, and RNAseq results.

claim: GTE-EGCG treatment modulated most systems simultaneously but did not rescue DS phenotypes.
source: GTE-EGCG treatment modulated most systems simultaneously but did not rescue DS phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple systems analyzed in the study including structural, functional, molecular, and genetic assessments.

claim: GTE-EGCG treatment exacerbated trisomic phenotypes including body weight, tibia microarchitecture, neurodevelopment, adult cognition, and metabolite concentration.
source: On the contrary, the treatment exacerbated trisomic phenotypes including body weight, tibia microarchitecture, neurodevelopment, adult cognition, and metabolite concentration, not supporting the therapeutic use of GTE-EGCG as a prenatal chronic treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from body weight measurements, µCT scans, behavioral tests, and MRS analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ts65Dn mouse model was one of the first preclinical models available for DS and has been widely used for experimental testing.
source: Much of this DS research was based on the Ts65Dn mouse model (Davisson et al., 1990; Reeves et al., 1995), as it was one of the first preclinical models available for DS and has been widely used for experimental testing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original publications describing the Ts65Dn mouse model.

claim: Ts65Dn mice carry a segment with approximately 120 genes homologous to Hsa21 translocated to a small centromeric part of Mmu17.
source: These mice carry a segment with approximately 120 genes homologous to Hsa21 (starting upstream of Mrpl39 to the telomeric end of Mmu16), translocated to a small centromeric part of Mmu17 (Duchon et al., 2011; Herault et al., 2017; Reinholdt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous genetic characterization studies of the Ts65Dn mouse model.

claim: Ts65Dn mice are trisomic for about two-thirds of the genes orthologous to Hsa21.
source: Ts65Dn mice are trisomic for about two-thirds of the genes orthologous to Hsa21, but also carry genes originating from the Mmu17 that are not related with DS, including about 46 protein-coding genes, 35 nonprotein-coding genes and 35 pseudogenes (Muñiz Moreno et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genetic characterization study.

claim: The Ts65Dn mouse model recapitulates the main skeletal, brain, cognitive, brain metabolite, and genetic alterations associated with DS.
source: However, in this study, we used the Ts65Dn mouse model because it recapitulates the main skeletal, brain, cognitive, brain metabolite, and genetic alterations associated with DS (Blazek et al., 2011; Costa et al., 2010; Dierssen et al., 2002; Escorihuela et al., 1998; Gupta et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2000; Llambrich et al., 2022b; Même et al., 2014; Starbuck et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies characterizing the Ts65Dn mouse model.

claim: People with DS show skeletal and brain alterations that progress through ontogeny.
source: At the structural level, people with DS show skeletal and brain alterations that progress through ontogeny (Antonarakis et al., 2020; de Moraes et al., 2008; Fischer-Brandies et al., 1986; Keeling et al., 1997; LaCombe and Roper, 2020; Pearlson et al., 1998; Starbuck et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies of DS.

claim: Children with DS have a decreased buildup of bone mass and a low bone turnover rate, resulting in more osteoclast than osteoblast activity, smaller bone area, lower bone mineral density (BMD), and an increased risk of osteoporosis at adulthood.
source: Children with DS have a decreased buildup of bone mass and a low bone turnover rate, resulting in more osteoclast than osteoblast activity, smaller bone area, lower bone mineral density (BMD), and an increased risk of osteoporosis at adulthood (Carfì et al., 2017; Keeling et al., 1997; LaCombe and Roper, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies of bone development in DS.

claim: Individuals with DS present midfacial hypoplasia and flattened nasal bridge along with skull malformations resulting in a shorter, wider, and rounder skull.
source: Individuals with DS also present midfacial hypoplasia and flattened nasal bridge along with skull malformations resulting in a shorter, wider, and rounder skull (Blazek et al., 2011; LaCombe and Roper, 2020; Richtsmeier et al., 2000; Suri et al., 2010; Thomas and Roper, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical and preclinical studies of craniofacial morphology in DS.

claim: A dose of 100 mg/kg/day of GTE-EGCG exacerbated facial dysmorphologies in Ts65Dn mice.
source: A dose of 100 mg/kg/day of GTE-EGCG exacerbated facial dysmorphologies (Starbuck et al., 2021), modified the skeletal dysmorphologies associated with DS without rescuing the bones shape (Llambrich et al., 2022a), and altered the integration between the skull and the brain (Llambrich et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A lower dose of 30 mg/kg/day of GTE-EGCG significantly reduced the facial dysmorphologies in Ts65Dn mice.
source: However, a lower dose of 30 mg/kg/day significantly reduced the facial dysmorphologies (Starbuck et al., 2021) but did not show additional rescuing effects in other skeletal traits (Llambrich et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: People with DS show a reduced overall brain volume from birth, with disproportionately smaller hippocampus and cerebellum, and larger ventricles.
source: People with DS show a reduced overall brain volume from birth, with disproportionately smaller hippocampus and cerebellum, and larger ventricles (Hamner et al., 2018; Movsas et al., 2016; Patkee et al., 2020; Pinter et al., 2001; Rodrigues et al., 2019; Smigielska-Kuzia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical neuroimaging studies of DS.

claim: Administration of 100 mg/kg/day of GTE-EGCG altered the brain shape of Ts65Dn mice at adulthood.
source: Our own previous study showed that administration of 100 mg/kg/day of GTE-EGCG altered the brain shape of Ts65Dn mice at adulthood (Llambrich et al., 2022b)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Administering green tea polyphenols corresponding to 0.6–1 mg EGCG per day in YACtg152F7 mice showed reduced thalamic-hypothalamic volume and reduced overall brain weight and volume.
source: while another study administering green tea polyphenols corresponding to 0.6–1 mg EGCG per day in YACtg152F7 mice showed reduced thalamic-hypothalamic volume and reduced overall brain weight and volume (Guedj et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: People with DS show relative impairment in executive function, short-term memory, working memory, and explicit long-term memory.
source: People with DS show relative impairment in executive function, short-term memory, working memory, and explicit long-term memory (Grieco et al., 2015; Lott and Dierssen, 2010; McCarron et al., 2017; Real de Asua et al., 2015; Steingass et al., 2011; Zis and Strydom, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical cognitive studies of DS.

claim: People with DS show a neurodevelopmental delay in the acquisition of both gross and fine motor skills during childhood.
source: together with a neurodevelopmental delay in the acquisition of both gross and fine motor skills during childhood (Beqaj et al., 2017; Ferreira-Vasques and Lamônica, 2015; Frank and Esbensen, 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Malak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical developmental studies of DS.

claim: A study administering 60 mg/kg GTE-EGCG to 3- to 4-month-old mBACtgDyrk1a and Ts65Dn mice for 4 weeks rescued working memory.
source: A study administering 60 mg/kg GTE-EGCG to 3- to 4-month-old mBACtgDyrk1a and Ts65Dn mice for 4 weeks rescued working memory (Souchet et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous preclinical study.

claim: Interventional studies in humans with DS have shown the ability of (GTE-)EGCG to improve memory recognition, working memory, inhibitory control, and adaptive behavior.
source: and interventional studies in humans with DS have shown the ability of (GTE-)EGCG to improve memory recognition, working memory, inhibitory control, and adaptive behavior (de la Torre et al., 2016; De la Torre et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical intervention studies.

claim: A randomized phase Ib clinical trial administering 10 mg/kg/day of EGCG for 6 months combined with a dietary supplement did not improve cognition and functionality in children aged 6–12 years with DS.
source: In children aged 6–12 years, a randomized phase Ib clinical trial administering 10 mg/kg/day of EGCG for 6 months combined with a dietary supplement did not improve cognition and functionality (Cieuta-Walti et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a clinical trial.

claim: GTE-EGCG at a dose of 30 mg/kg/day had no effect on visuospatial learning and memory, and even resulted in reduced swimming speed in the Morris water maze and increased thigmotaxic behavior in 5- to 6-month-old Ts65Dn mice.
source: In mice, GTE-EGCG at a dose of 30 mg/kg/day had no effect on visuospatial learning and memory, and even resulted in reduced swimming speed in the Morris water maze and increased thigmotaxic behavior in 5- to 6-month-old Ts65Dn mice (Catuara-Solarz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous preclinical study.

claim: People with DS show increased myo-inositol levels when compared to euploid population.
source: Several studies have shown that the cognitive functional alterations observed in DS are related with changes at a molecular level on the concentration of hippocampal metabolites, as people with DS show increased myo-inositol levels when compared to euploid population, and people with DS and dementia show reduced levels of N-acetylaspartate (NAA) when compared to people with DS without dementia (Beacher et al., 2005; Lamar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical MRS studies.

claim: People with DS and dementia show reduced levels of N-acetylaspartate (NAA) when compared to people with DS without dementia.
source: Several studies have shown that the cognitive functional alterations observed in DS are related with changes at a molecular level on the concentration of hippocampal metabolites, as people with DS show increased myo-inositol levels when compared to euploid population, and people with DS and dementia show reduced levels of N-acetylaspartate (NAA) when compared to people with DS without dementia (Beacher et al., 2005; Lamar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical MRS studies.

claim: Skeletal malformations can be associated with the dysregulation of genes such as RCAN1, SOD1, EN2, ETS2, SHH, DYRK1A, SOX9, and OTX2.
source: Indeed, skeletal malformations can be associated with the dysregulation of genes such as Regulator of Calcineurin 1 (RCAN1), Superoxide Dismutase 1 (SOD1), Engrailed Homeobox 2 (EN2), ETS Proto-Oncogene 2 (ETS2), Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Dual-Specificity Tyrosine-(Y)-Phosphorylation Regulated Kinase 1 A (DYRK1A), SRY-Box Transcription Factor 9 (SOX9), and Orthodenticle Homeobox 2 (OTX2) (Arron et al., 2006; Billingsley et al., 2013; McElyea et al., 2016; Roper et al., 2009; Thomas and Roper, 2021; Weisfeld-Adams et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Cognitive impairment and altered brain development may be associated with RCAN1, SOD1, OLIG1, OLIG2, SIM2, DSCAM, DYRK1A, DSCR1, SYNJ1 and KCNJ6.
source: while cognitive impairment and altered brain development may be associated with RCAN1, SOD1, Oligodendrocyte Transcription Factor 1 (OLIG1), Oligodendrocyte Transcription Factor2 (OLIG2), SIM BHLH Transcription Factor 2 (SIM2), Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule (DSCAM), DYRK1A, Down Syndrome Critical Region 1 (DSCR1), Synaptojanin 1 (SYNJ1) and Potassium Inwardly Rectifying Channel Subfamily J Member 6 (KCNJ6) (Chang et al., 2003; Hoeffer et al., 2007; Kazemi et al., 2016; Kleschevnikov et al., 2017; Lana-Elola et al., 2011; Stagni and Bartesaghi, 2022; Stagni et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic and molecular studies.

claim: DYRK1A has been proposed as a target gene for therapy in DS.
source: From these genes, DYRK1A, a gene involved in both skeletal and neuronal development that is overexpressed by trisomy of chromosome 21 (Blazek et al., 2015a; Dierssen and de Lagrán, 2006), has been proposed as a target gene for therapy (Atas-Ozcan et al., 2021; Becker et al., 2014; Dierssen and de Lagrán, 2006; García-Cerro et al., 2014; Jarhad et al., 2018; Ji et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2009; Rondal, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to therapeutic development studies.

claim: A study administering 200 mg/kg EGCG on embryonic days 7 and 8 twice daily showed decreases in Ptch and Ets2 RNA expression and significant increases in Rcan1 and Shh RNA expression in the first pharyngeal arch of Ts65Dn mice at embryonic day 9.5.
source: The potential of EGCG to modulate gene expression in the Ts65Dn mouse model for DS has limited evidence, with one study administering 200 mg/kg EGCG on embryonic days 7 and 8 twice daily showing decreases in Protein patched homolog 1 (Ptch) and Ets2 RNA expression and significant increases in Rcan1 and Shh RNA expression in the first pharyngeal arch of Ts65Dn mice at embryonic day (E) 9.5 (McElyea et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous gene expression study.

claim: TS untreated mice tended to present lower body weights than WT untreated mice over development from birth to adulthood, but these genotype differences did not reach significance at any developmental stage.
source: TS untreated mice tended to present lower body weights than WT untreated mice over development from birth to adulthood, but these genotype differences did not reach significance at any developmental stage (Figure 2A; PBW1=0.7630; PBW2=0.3688; PBW3=0.1094).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: Chronic GTE-EGCG treatment significantly reduced the body growth of TS treated mice from PD1 to PD17 in comparison with WT untreated, WT treated, and TS untreated mice.
source: Chronic GTE-EGCG treatment, which started prenatally and was maintained until 5 months, significantly reduced the body growth of TS treated mice from PD1 to PD17 (Figure 2A at BW1) in comparison with WT untreated (p<0.0001), WT treated (p<0.0001), and TS untreated mice (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: At adulthood before treatment discontinuation, TS treated mice showed significantly different body weight when compared to WT untreated and WT treated mice.
source: At adulthood before treatment discontinuation (Figure 2A at BW2), these differences were maintained, but only reached significance when compared to WT untreated (p=0.0322) and WT treated mice (p=0.0103).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: After three months of treatment discontinuation, both WT and TS treated mice showed a mild increase in body weight.
source: After three months of treatment discontinuation, both WT and TS treated mice showed a mild increase in body weight, making TS treated mice not significantly different from WT untreated (Figure 2A; PBW3=0.9284), and causing WT treated mice to be significantly different from WT untreated (Figure 2A; PBW3=0.0259).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: TS untreated mice presented a significantly different craniofacial shape than WT untreated mice at µCT1 and µCT2.
source: The results confirmed our previous findings (Llambrich et al., 2022a; Llambrich et al., 2022b), showing that TS untreated mice presented a significantly different craniofacial shape than WT untreated mice at µCT1 (p<0.0001) and µCT2 (p=0.0011) (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from geometric morphometric analysis of µCT scans with statistical analysis.

claim: The craniofacial differences induced by genotype persisted until adulthood.
source: In this study, we further detected that the craniofacial differences induced by genotype persisted until adulthood (Figure 2B and PµCT3=0.0009; Figure 2C and PµCT4=0.0055).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from geometric morphometric analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Prenatal chronic GTE-EGCG treatment only showed a significant effect in the craniofacial shape at PD3, where both WT and TS treated mice were different from their untreated counterparts.
source: Prenatal chronic GTE-EGCG treatment only showed a significant effect in the craniofacial shape at PD3, where both WT and TS treated mice were different from their untreated counterparts (PWT=0.0418; PTS=0.0005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from geometric morphometric analysis with statistical analysis.

claim: The treatment never rescued the craniofacial shape in TS treated mice, as these mice were significantly different from WT untreated mice at all stages.
source: However, the treatment never rescued the craniofacial shape in TS treated mice, as these mice were significantly different from WT untreated mice at all stages (Figure 2B and C; Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from geometric morphometric analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Discontinuing the treatment for three months did not induce any effects on craniofacial shape, maintaining the craniofacial dysmorphologies already observed at µCT3.
source: Discontinuing the treatment for three months did not induce any effects (Figure 2C), maintaining the craniofacial dysmorphologies already observed at µCT3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from geometric morphometric analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: TS untreated mice tended to present lower BMD than WT untreated mice over development and adulthood, but the differences did not reach significance at any developmental stage.
source: Although we observed that TS untreated mice tended to present lower BMD than WT untreated mice over development and adulthood, the differences did not reach significance at any developmental stage (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BMD measurements shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: Prenatal GTE-EGCG chronic treatment significantly modified the developmental trajectory of humerus BMD in WT and TS treated mice.
source: Prenatal GTE-EGCG chronic treatment significantly modified the developmental trajectory of humerus BMD in WT and TS treated mice (PWT <0.0001; PTS=0.0023), but never rescued the trisomic phenotype, as TS treated mice remained different from WT untreated (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BMD measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: After 3 months of treatment discontinuation, both WT and TS treated groups showed a decline in BMD, which caused WT and TS treated mice to be different than WT untreated control mice.
source: This tendency for reduced BMD was rescued at adulthood (Figure 2D at µCT3), but after 3 months of treatment discontinuation, both WT and TS treated groups showed a decline in BMD (Figure 2D at µCT4), which caused WT and TS treated mice to be different than WT untreated control mice (PWT=0.0001; PTS=0.0002), suggesting a rebound effect following treatment retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BMD measurements shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: The LDA of tibia microarchitecture showed limited overlap between groups, as mice separated by treatment along the first axis, and by genotype along the second axis.
source: The LDA showed limited overlap between groups, as mice separated by treatment along the first axis, and by genotype along the second axis. These results suggested genotype differences and treatment effects that did not rescue the trisomic phenotype (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TS untreated mice tended to show specific reductions in cortical thickness, polar moment of inertia, cross-sectional area, and bone area.
source: Even though we did not detect any significant difference between WT untreated and TS untreated mice in any structural domain (Supplementary file 2c), TS untreated mice tended to show specific reductions in cortical thickness, polar moment of inertia, cross-sectional area, and bone area (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 C,E,F,G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tibia microarchitecture measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TS untreated mice showed significantly reduced tibia length and periosteal perimeter compared to WT untreated mice.
source: and the univariate pairwise comparison tests revealed significant differences in the tibia length (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; p=0.0170) and periosteal perimeter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I; p=0.0154).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tibia measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: After GTE-EGCG chronic treatment and discontinuation, WT treated mice showed significantly reduced tibia length and cortical porosity, together with increased cortical BMD compared to WT untreated mice.
source: After GTE-EGCG chronic treatment and discontinuation, WT treated mice were not significantly different than WT untreated mice for any specific structural domain (Supplementary file 2c), but the univariate pairwise tests indicated significantly reduced tibia length (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; p=0.0006) and cortical porosity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; p=0.0120), together with increased cortical BMD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; p=0.0120).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tibia microarchitecture measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: TS treated mice showed significantly more mineralized, thicker, and less porous cortical bone compared to TS untreated mice.
source: TS treated mice were significantly different than TS untreated mice for the cortical bone strength and cortical bone size domains (Supplementary file 2c), showing significantly more mineralized (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; p=0.0039), thicker (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; p=0.0400), and less porous (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; p=0.0005) cortical bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tibia microarchitecture measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: The LDA including the volumes of subcortical brain regions showed genotype separation across Axis 1 at MRI1, which further increased at MRI2.
source: The LDA including the volumes of the subcortical brain regions mentioned above showed genotype separation across Axis 1 at MRI1, which further increased at MRI2, with WT mice occupying the negative extreme of Axis 1 and TS mice occupying the positive extreme (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: Multivariate pairwise comparisons confirmed genotype differences only at MRI2, when WT untreated mice were significantly different than TS untreated.
source: The multivariate pairwise comparisons after one-way PERMANOVA using Mahalanobis distances (Supplementary file 2d and e) confirmed genotype differences only at MRI2, when WT untreated mice were significantly different than TS untreated (Figure 2G; p=0.0065).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis with results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Adult TS untreated mice tended to present larger volumes than WT untreated mice in all brain regions at both MRI1 and MRI2.
source: Contrary to previous evidence in Ts65Dn mice (Aldridge et al., 2007; Duchon et al., 2021; Holtzman et al., 1996; Insausti et al., 1998), adult TS untreated mice tended to present larger volumes than WT untreated mice in all brain regions at both MRI1 and MRI2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from brain volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and contrasts with previous studies cited.

claim: TS mice presented a significantly larger brain, hippocampal region and whole ventricles volume than WT untreated mice at MRI1.
source: The univariate pairwise tests performed at MRI1 confirmed that TS mice presented a significantly larger brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, top; p=0.0066), hippocampal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, top; p=0.0254) and whole ventricles volume (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H, top; p=0.0427) than WT untreated mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from brain volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: At MRI2, TS untreated mice showed significant increases in the volumes of the third ventricle and fourth ventricle compared to WT untreated mice.
source: At MRI2, these differences did no longer reach significance and significant increases emerged in the volumes of the third ventricle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, bottom; p=0.0479) and fourth ventricle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F, bottom; p=0.0014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from brain volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: The LDA at MRI1 showed separation between TS treated mice and the rest of the groups.
source: Regarding treatment effects, the LDA at MRI1 showed separation between TS treated mice and the rest of the groups (Figure 2F), and the multivariate pairwise comparisons after one-way PERMANOVA confirmed significant differences between WT untreated and TS treated mice (p=0.0047), but not between TS untreated and TS treated mice (p=0.4921).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figure 2F with statistical analysis.

claim: TS treated mice showed a significantly larger hippocampal region than TS untreated mice at MRI1.
source: Indeed, TS treated mice tended to show larger volumes than TS untreated mice in all brain regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), but the univariate pairwise comparison tests only detected a significant difference in the hippocampal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, top; p=0.0413).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from brain volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: After 3 months of treatment discontinuation at MRI2, TS treated mice remained significantly different than WT untreated mice in all univariate brain regions except for the volume of the third ventricle.
source: After 3 months of treatment discontinuation at MRI2, some TS treated mice tended to occupy the same space as WT untreated mice in the LDA (Figure 2G), and although the multivariate pairwise comparisons after one-way PERMANOVA did not detect significant differences between WT untreated and TS treated mice (p=0.0609), TS treated mice remained significantly different than WT untreated mice in all univariate brain regions except for the volume of the third ventricle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, bottom; p=0.0562), indicating limited rescuing effects at this last stage after treatment discontinuation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from brain volumetric measurements shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: The LDA with the results from all neurodevelopmental tests combined showed that the treatment was the main differentiating factor among groups of mice.
source: The LDA with the results from all neurodevelopmental tests combined showed that the treatment was the main differentiating factor among groups of mice, as Axis 1 separated treated and untreated mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Multivariate pairwise comparisons detected significant differences between TS untreated and WT untreated mice, and between TS treated mice and both TS untreated and WT untreated mice in neurodevelopmental tests.
source: The multivariate pairwise comparisons after one-way PERMANOVA using Mahalanobis distances (Supplementary file 2f) detected significant differences between TS untreated and WT untreated mice (p=0.0001), and between TS treated mice and both TS untreated (p=0.0001) and WT untreated mice (p=0.0001), confirming these findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Multivariate pairwise comparisons only indicated significant differences between WT untreated and TS untreated mice for the reflexes domain in neurodevelopmental tests.
source: When the neurodevelopmental tests were grouped into functional domains (developmental landmarks, neuromotor tests and reflexes) (Supplementary file 2f), the multivariate pairwise comparisons only indicated significant differences between WT untreated and TS untreated mice for the reflexes (p=0.0423).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: TS untreated mice showed significant delays in the acquisition rate of the vertical climbing and tactile response, together with the average day of acquisition of the surface righting response.
source: TS untreated mice tended to be delayed in most individual tests (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the univariate pairwise comparison tests confirmed significant delays in the acquisition rate of the vertical climbing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; p=0.0256) and tactile response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I; p=0.0064), together with the average day of acquisition of the surface righting response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; p=0.0320).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neurodevelopmental tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: TS untreated mice tended to be anticipated in the vibrissae placing, blast response, and Preyer reflex, although these results did not reach significance.
source: However, we also observed that TS untreated mice tended to be anticipated in the vibrissae placing, blast response, and Preyer reflex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 J,M,N), even though these results did not reach significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neurodevelopmental tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prenatal chronic treatment with GTE-EGCG caused TS treated mice to be significantly different than TS untreated mice for the domains neuromotor tests and reflexes.
source: Prenatal chronic treatment with GTE-EGCG caused TS treated mice to be significantly different than TS untreated mice for the domains neuromotor tests and reflexes, and WT treated mice to be different from WT untreated mice for the domain reflexes (Supplementary file 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Treatment significantly modulated the average day of acquisition and acquisition rate of multiple neurodevelopmental tests in both WT and TS treated mice, causing either a delay or an anticipation in most tests.
source: The univariate tests indicated that treatment significantly modulated the average day of acquisition and acquisition rate of multiple neurodevelopmental tests in both WT and TS treated mice, causing either a delay or an anticipation in most tests (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neurodevelopmental tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All Ts65Dn mothers performed similarly and there was no large intra-group variation for any of the behaviors analyzed, confirming that maternal care did not influence the results of the neurodevelopmental tests.
source: Finally, we investigated the mothers' behavior during 24 hr at PD8 to evaluate maternal care and observed that, despite being trisomic, all Ts65Dn mothers performed similarly and there was no large intra-group variation for any of the behaviors analyzed, confirming that maternal care did not influence the results of the neurodevelopmental tests (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from maternal care observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant differences were detected between treated and untreated mothers in any maternal care behavior, confirming that the GTE-EGCG treatment did not modulate maternal care.
source: Furthermore, no significant differences were detected between treated and untreated mothers in any readout (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), confirming that the GTE-EGCG treatment did not modulate maternal care.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from maternal care observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The LDA with the results from all adult cognitive tests combined showed minor overlap between groups at both Cog.1 and Cog.2.
source: The LDA with the results from all tests combined showed minor overlap between groups at both Cog.1 and Cog.2 (Figure 3B and C), with WT untreated mice occupying the negative extreme of Axis 1, WT treated and TS untreated mice presenting an intermediate position, and TS treated mice falling on the positive extreme of Axis 1, opposite to WT untreated mice (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Multivariate pairwise comparisons confirmed significant genotype differences between WT and TS untreated mice at Cog.1 but not at Cog.2.
source: These results suggested genotype differences between WT and TS untreated mice that were confirmed as significant by the multivariate pairwise comparisons after one-way PERMANOVA at Cog.1 (Supplementary file 2g; p=0.0125) but not at Cog.2 (Supplementary file 2h; p=0.4596).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Multivariate pairwise comparisons only detected a significant difference between WT untreated and TS untreated mice for the arousal tests at Cog.1.
source: When the cognitive tests were grouped into cognitive domains (anxiety, arousal, and memory), the multivariate pairwise comparisons only detected a significant difference between WT untreated and TS untreated mice for the arousal tests at Cog.1 (p=0.0028) (Supplementary file 2g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: TS untreated mice showed a tendency to cover longer distances at higher speed in all arousal tests when compared with WT untreated mice.
source: Indeed, TS untreated mice showed a tendency to cover longer distances at higher speed in all arousal tests when compared with WT untreated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 E-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: TS untreated mice showed significantly increased distance and speed during OF, as well as distance and speed during NOR at Cog.1.
source: These differences reached significance for the distance and speed during OF, as well as for the distance and speed during NOR at Cog.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 E,F,I,J, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: TS untreated mice showed impaired memory robustness and formation at the latest stage, with significantly less preference for the novel object during NOR when compared with WT untreated mice.
source: Finally, TS untreated mice showed impaired memory robustness and formation at the latest stage, with significantly less preference for the novel object during NOR when compared with WT untreated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3K, bottom; p=0.0257), and a tendency for reduced latency to enter the dark chamber during training and testing sessions for PA at Cog.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 M,N, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: WT treated mice were significantly different than WT untreated mice when all cognitive tests were considered together as well as for the anxiety and arousal domains at Cog.1.
source: Indeed, WT treated mice were significantly different than WT untreated mice when all cognitive tests were considered together as well as for the anxiety and arousal domains (Supplementary file 2g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Both WT and TS treated mice showed significantly increased time in the center during NOR, and increased time in the open arm during EPM at Cog.1 when compared with WT untreated mice.
source: Both WT and TS treated mice showed significantly increased time in the center during NOR, and increased time in the open arm during EPM at Cog.1 when compared with WT untreated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 C,D, top), indicating increased exploratory and risk-taking behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both WT and TS treated mice covered significantly more distance at more speed than WT untreated mice for the distance and speed during OF, as well as the distance and speed during NOR at Cog.1.
source: Similarly, both WT and TS treated mice showed increased locomotor activity, as they covered significantly more distance at more speed than WT untreated mice for the distance and speed during OF, as well as the distance and speed during NOR at Cog.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 E,F,I,J, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: TS treated mice had greater preference for the novel stranger (S2) than TS untreated mice at Cog.1.
source: However, in the memory tests (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 K-N), the pairwise comparison tests revealed only a significant difference between TS untreated and TS treated mice for the preference for subject 2 (S2) at Cog.1, where treated mice had greater preference for the novel stranger (Figure 3—figure supplement 3L, top; p=0.0137).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: After treatment discontinuation at Cog.2, the LDA presented a similar pattern as at Cog.1, suggesting that discontinuing the treatment for one month did not substantially change the cognitive patterns induced after chronic GTE-EGCG treatment.
source: After treatment discontinuation at Cog.2, the LDA (Figure 3C) presented a similar pattern as the LDA at Cog.1 (Figure 3B), suggesting that discontinuing the treatment for one month did not substantially change the cognitive patterns induced after chronic GTE-EGCG treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3C with inference.

claim: New significant differences emerged between WT untreated and both WT treated and TS treated mice when evaluating the memory domain at Cog.2.
source: However, new significant differences emerged between WT untreated and both WT treated and TS treated mice when evaluating the memory domain (Supplementary file 2h), suggesting that the treatment discontinuation altered the memory of both WT and TS mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis with inference.

claim: TS treated mice remained significantly different than WT untreated mice for all tests combined and all cognitive domains at Cog.2.
source: Furthermore, TS treated mice remained significantly different than WT untreated mice for all tests combined and all cognitive domains (Supplementary file 2h), confirming that the effects of treatment discontinuation did not rescue the trisomic cognitive phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Both treated groups showed hyperactivity as TS treated mice were significantly different from WT untreated mice for all arousal tests at Cog.2.
source: A similar trend was observed for the arousal tests, as even though no significant differences were detected between TS treated and TS untreated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-J, bottom), both treated groups showed hyperactivity as the univariate pairwise comparison tests confirmed significant differences between TS treated mice and WT untreated mice for all arousal tests (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-J, bottom)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: TS treated mice were significantly different than TS untreated but not than WT untreated mice for the preference for the novel object during NOR at Cog.2.
source: In the memory tests, TS treated mice were significantly different than TS untreated (p=0.0046) but not than WT untreated mice for the preference for the novel object during NOR (Figure 3—figure supplement 3K, bottom; p=0.3566), which could suggest a beneficial treatment effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis and speculation about beneficial effects.

claim: WT untreated mice did not enter the dark box during training at Cog.2, while both WT and TS treated mice showed a reduced tendency to enter the dark chamber.
source: Indeed, WT untreated mice did not enter the dark box during training at Cog.2, while both WT and TS treated mice showed a reduced tendency to enter the dark chamber which reached significance when comparing TS treated mice with WT untreated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3M, bottom; p<0.0001), indicating less robust contextual memory retention.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: The LDA at MRS1 separated WT untreated and TS untreated mice across Axis 1.
source: The LDA at MRS1 separated WT untreated and TS untreated mice across Axis 1 (Figure 4A), and the multivariate pairwise comparisons after one-way PERMANOVA using Mahalanobis distances confirmed significant genotype differences (Supplementary file 2i; p=0.0136).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figure 4A with statistical analysis.

claim: After treatment discontinuation at MRS2, the LDA showed milder genotype separation and the multivariate pairwise comparisons did not detect any significant difference between WT untreated and TS untreated mice.
source: After treatment discontinuation at MRS2, the LDA showed milder genotype separation (Figure 4B) and the multivariate pairwise comparisons did not detect any significant difference between WT untreated and TS untreated mice (Supplementary file 2j; p=0.5790), confirming these findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: TS untreated mice showed a significant increase in the concentration of Cr +PCr at MRS1 compared to WT untreated mice.
source: TS untreated mice tended to show lower levels of NAA and tCho at MRS1 when compared with WT untreated mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 A,C), but the univariate pairwise comparison tests only revealed a significant increase in the concentration of Cr +PCr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, top; p=0.0235).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MRS measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: The LDA at MRS1 separated treated and untreated mice across Axis 2, suggesting treatment effects that did not rescue the trisomic phenotype.
source: Regarding treatment effects, the LDA at MRS1 separated treated and untreated mice across Axis 2 (Figure 4A), suggesting treatment effects that did not rescue the trisomic phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA analysis shown in Figure 4A with inference.

claim: TS treated mice showed significantly increased levels of Cr +PCr and reduced tCho levels compared with WT untreated mice at MRS1.
source: When evaluating the specific concentrations of NAA, Cr +PCr, tCho, myo-Inos and Tau, both WT treated and TS treated mice tended to show increased levels of Cr +PCr, which reached significance when comparing TS treated mice with WT untreated mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, top; p=0.0317). Conversely, both WT and TS treated mice tended to show reduced levels of myo-inositol and tCho (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, top), causing TS treated mice to have significantly reduced tCho when compared with WT untreated mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, top; p=0.0296).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MRS measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: After treatment discontinuation at MRS2, the differences between TS treated and WT untreated mice remained significant in the LDA but not in specific metabolite concentrations.
source: After treatment discontinuation at MRS2, the LDA showed milder treatment separation across Axis 2 (Figure 4B) and the multivariate pairwise comparisons did not detect any significant difference between TS untreated and TS treated mice (Supplementary file 2j; p=0.2111). However, the differences between TS treated and WT untreated mice remained significant (p=0.0347), indicating that discontinuing the treatment for 3 months did not rescue the trisomic phenotype. When evaluating the specific concentrations of NAA, Cr +PCr, tCho, myo-Inos and Tau, the same pattern was observed and the significant differences between TS treated and WT untreated mice disappeared (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LDA and MRS measurements shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Significant differences emerged between WT untreated mice and WT treated mice for the concentration of tCho and myo-inositol at MRS2.
source: However, significant differences emerged between WT untreated mice and WT treated mice for the concentration of tCho and myo-inositol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 C,D, bottom; PtCho=0.0479, Pmyo-inositol=0.0261).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MRS measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: The PCA using the normalized expression of the 125 genes that are triplicated in the Ts65Dn mouse model showed major overlap between all groups.
source: We first performed a PCA using the normalized expression of the 125 genes that are triplicated in the Ts65Dn mouse model and included in our dataset. The PCA showed major overlap between all groups, even though TS treated mice showed a larger range of variation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PCA analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The differences in gene expression of the triplicated genes were minimal and GTE-EGCG prenatal chronic treatment and three months of discontinuation did not induce major permanent effects when considering all triplicated genes.
source: This result suggested that the differences in gene expression of the triplicated genes were minimal and that GTE-EGCG prenatal chronic treatment and three months of discontinuation did not induce major permanent effects when considering all triplicated genes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the PCA results showing overlap between groups.

claim: Only 24 DEGs were detected between WT untreated and TS untreated mice when analyzing the entire transcriptome, indicating small differences in cerebellar gene expression.
source: When analyzing the entire transcriptome, we only detected 24 DEGs between WT untreated and TS untreated mice even when applying a loose p-adjusted value of 0.1, indicating small differences in cerebellar gene expression (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis.

claim: 12 DEGs were detected between WT untreated and TS treated mice, and only 9 of these genes were also found to be differentially expressed between WT untreated and TS untreated mice, which could indicate mild treatment effects in TS mice.
source: Interestingly, we detected 12 DEGs between WT untreated and TS treated mice, and only 9 of these genes were also found to be differentially expressed between WT untreated and TS untreated mice, which could indicate mild treatment effects in TS mice (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis with speculation about treatment effects.

claim: No DEGs were detected between TS untreated and TS treated mice, and only five DEGs were detected between WT untreated and WT treated mice.
source: However, we did not detect any DEGs between TS untreated and TS treated mice, and only five DEGs were detected between WT untreated and WT treated mice, indicating that either the prenatal chronic GTE-EGCG treatment did not largely modulate gene expression or that the treatment had transient effects that were mostly not detected after three months of treatment discontinuation and were not rescuing the trisomic phenotype (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis with speculation about the interpretation.

claim: TS untreated mice presented mild gene expression alterations in the cerebellum but still showed hyperactivity and increased cerebellar volume.
source: For example, we observed that even though TS untreated mice presented mild gene expression alterations in the cerebellum, these mice still showed hyperactivity and increased cerebellar volume.
evidence: This claim integrates data from multiple experiments (RNAseq, behavior, MRI) to make an inference about the relationship between molecular and phenotypic changes.

claim: The altered expression of a few genes was sufficient to alter the brain and cognitive phenotypes, or the alteration of gene expression during development was no longer detected at adulthood but was sufficient to permanently alter brain volumetry and cognition.
source: These results can be interpreted as that the altered expression of a few genes was sufficient to alter the brain and cognitive phenotypes, or that the alteration of gene expression during development was no longer detected at adulthood but was sufficient to permanently alter brain volumetry and cognition, which would be in line with previous reports indicating that the altered phenotype in DS was due to small contributions of multiple genes rather than strong effects of a few selected genes (Antonarakis et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2020; Chrast et al., 2000; De Toma et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trisomy altered the expression of genes related with hypotonia and movement impairment such as Son, Synj1, Atp5o, Jam2, and Paxbp1, but TS mice still showed increased locomotor activity.
source: Interestingly, trisomy altered the expression of genes related with hypotonia and movement impairment such as Son, Synj1, Atp5o, Jam2, and Paxbp1; but TS mice still showed increased locomotor activity.
evidence: This claim integrates data from RNAseq and behavioral tests to make an observation about the relationship between gene expression and phenotype.

claim: The cognitive differences induced by both the genotype and treatment were not related with the concentration of NAA in the hippocampal region but rather with general differences in hippocampal region volume and metabolite spectra.
source: These results suggested that the cognitive differences induced by both the genotype and treatment were not related with the concentration of NAA in the hippocampal region but rather with general differences in hippocampal region volume and metabolite spectra.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from integrating data from MRS, MRI, and behavioral tests.

claim: The Ts65Dn model reflects the multisystemic nature of DS and recapitulates many characteristics of the trisomic phenotype.
source: Our results support that, overall, the Ts65Dn model reflects the multisystemic nature of DS and recapitulates many characteristics of the trisomic phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comprehensive experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Ts65Dn mice did not show altered tibia microarchitecture and showed increased hippocampal, cerebellar, ventricular, and whole brain volumes, which do not match the human condition.
source: However, our results also revealed phenotypes that did not match the human condition, as Ts65Dn mice did not show altered tibia microarchitecture and showed increased hippocampal, cerebellar, ventricular, and whole brain volumes.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study and comparison with known human phenotypes.

claim: There is a genotypic and phenotypic drift within the Ts65Dn mouse model, as a decrease in the magnitude of alterations induced by the genotype was observed compared to previous articles.
source: Overall, our longitudinal analyses confirm the validity of the model for the structural, functional, molecular and genetic phenotypes associated with DS, but also support the hypothesis of genotypic and phenotypic drift within the Ts65Dn mouse model (Shaw et al., 2020), as we generally observed a decrease in the magnitude of alterations induced by the genotype compared to previous articles including our earlier work.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing current results with previous studies and is supported by a citation.

claim: GTE-EGCG modulated most systems simultaneously along development but did not rescue the trisomic phenotype and even exacerbated some phenotypes over time.
source: Regarding the treatment effects, our results confirmed that GTE-EGCG modulated most of these systems simultaneously along development. However, our holistic approach revealed that, in general, the treatment did not rescue the trisomic phenotype and even exacerbated some phenotypes over time, such as body weight, tibia microarchitecture, neurodevelopment, adult cognition, and hippocampal metabolite concentration.
evidence: This claim is based on comprehensive experimental data from multiple systems analyzed in the study.

claim: Discontinuing the GTE-EGCG administration reduced the treatment effects but did not rescue the trisomic phenotype.
source: Although discontinuing the GTE-EGCG administration reduced the treatment effects, it did not rescue the trisomic phenotype, as TS treated mice remained different from WT untreated mice in most systems.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from multiple systems analyzed after treatment discontinuation.

claim: Discontinuing the GTE-EGCG treatment for three months only rescued the body weight and brain volume of a few TS mice but increased the weight of WT mice and reduced the BMD of the humerus in both WT and TS mice.
source: Discontinuing the GTE-EGCG treatment for three months only rescued the body weight and brain volume of a few TS mice but increased the weight of WT mice and reduced the BMD of the humerus in both WT and TS mice.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from body weight, brain volume, and BMD measurements after treatment discontinuation.

claim: The preclinical results warn against a chronic GTE-EGCG treatment initiated prenatally and maintained until adulthood with a dosage of 30 mg/kg/day.
source: Summing up, our preclinical results warn against a chronic GTE-EGCG treatment initiated prenatally and maintained until adulthood with a dosage of 30 mg/kg/day.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comprehensive experimental data showing lack of rescue and exacerbation of phenotypes.

claim: EGCG crosses the placental barrier and reaches the embryo.
source: As EGCG crosses the placental barrier and reaches the embryo (Chu et al., 2006), GTE-EGCG treatment started prenatally at embryonic day 9 (E9) via the drinking water of the pregnant dams.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Maternal plasma concentrations of catechins are about 10 times higher than in placenta and 50–100 times higher than in the fetal brain.
source: In developing embryos and pups before weaning, the received dosage was lower since previous studies indicate that maternal plasma concentrations of catechins are about 10 times higher than in placenta and 50–100 times higher than in the fetal brain (Chu et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: EGCG in milk and plasma of PD1 to PD7 pups was detected at low concentrations.
source: and EGCG in milk and plasma of PD1 to PD7 pups was detected at low concentrations (Souchet et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An adult mouse weighing 20 g drinks approximately 6 mL of water per day.
source: The calculated dosage of EGCG received by an adult mouse would be approximately 30 mg/kg/day considering that, on average, early adult mice weigh 20 g and drink 6 mL of water per day according to our measurements.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements made by the authors in this study.

claim: The experimental pipeline used in this article is applicable to any rodent model and potential therapeutic compound.
source: The experimental pipeline used in this article, from the imaging techniques to the data analysis strategy, are applicable to any rodent model and potential therapeutic compound, allowing the integrated investigation of other therapeutic compounds and DS models that more faithfully replicate the genetic condition of DS, such as the TcHSA21rat and TcMAC21 mouse model (Kazuki et al., 2020; Kazuki et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the generalizability of the methods and is supported by citations to other DS models.
